overview: This file documents U.S.–Japanese negotiations and preparations for Richard Halliburton and aviator Moye W. Stephens Jr. to fly over Japanese-ruled Taiwan in 1931–1932. Japan offered permission subject to a prescribed route and regulations, while making it conditional upon reciprocal American authorization for a Japanese newspaper-sponsored aircraft bound for Australia to land at Manila. Later correspondence from the American consul at Xiamen transmitted a Japanese-provided map of a temporary Taiwan landing field but reported that the proposed Halliburton–Stephens flight had apparently been abandoned; the map was also passed to the U.S. Asiatic Fleet.

people.name: Richard Halliburton
people.role: American traveler and flier involved in the proposed flight over Taiwan

people.name: Moye W. Stephens Jr.
people.role: American aviator involved in the proposed flight over Taiwan; his surname is rendered “Stevens” in the file

subfiles.title: Cross-reference for Forbes telegram on the proposed Taiwan flight
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to another file for Forbes’s telegram concerning Japanese conditions for the Halliburton–Stephens flight over Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: This filing note summarizes Japan’s lack of objection to the proposed flight provided that the specified route and regulations were followed. Japanese consent was conditional upon permission for a Japanese aircraft flying from Japan to Australia to land at Manila.

subfiles.title: Forbes telegram on conditional Japanese approval of the Taiwan flight
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forbes reports that Japan would permit the Halliburton–Stephens flight if the United States granted landing rights at Manila to a Japanese aircraft.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese Foreign Office stated that it had no objection to the flight over Taiwan if its route and regulations were observed. Its approval was tied to American authorization for a Super Universal aircraft with a 420-horsepower Jupiter engine, sponsored by a Nagoya newspaper, to land at Manila during a Japan-to-Australia flight before April. Forbes requested instructions on where to forward the Japanese regulations once the Manila landing was approved.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference for Franklin’s report and landing-field map
subfiles.about: The sheet points to Franklin’s report concerning a map supplied for the proposed Halliburton–Stephens flight over Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: This filing note describes a map obtained from the Japanese consul at Xiamen for Halliburton and Stephens. The map showed a military drill ground prepared as a temporary landing field on Taiwan. The printed year “1938” is evidently an OCR or filing-form error for 1932, matching the report that follows.

subfiles.title: Franklin report No. 47 on the proposed flight to Taiwan
subfiles.from: Lynn W. Franklin, American Consul at Xiamen
subfiles.to: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Minister at Beijing
subfiles.about: Franklin forwards a Japanese map of a temporary Taiwan landing field and reports that the proposed flight apparently will not occur.
subfiles.summary: Responding to the legation’s instructions of February 15, Franklin enclosed a copy of a map supplied by the Japanese consul at Xiamen. The consul described the site as a military drill ground specially prepared as a temporary landing field for the two fliers. He subsequently told Franklin that Halliburton and Stephens had advised that the flight would not take place. Franklin also gave a copy to the commander of USS Stewart, who reportedly forwarded it to the commander-in-chief of the U.S. Asiatic Fleet.

subfiles.title: Map of landing field in Formosa
subfiles.about: The enclosure depicts the Taiwan landing field described in Franklin’s report.
subfiles.summary: The map is labeled “Landing Field - Formosa” and identifies the site as approximately 150 meters above sea level. Franklin’s accompanying report explains that it was a military drill ground temporarily prepared for Halliburton and Stephens.

interest: The file is valuable for showing how an ostensibly private adventure flight became entangled in diplomatic reciprocity, colonial airspace controls, and wider trans-Pacific aviation ambitions. Particularly notable is Japan’s attempt to exchange permission over Taiwan for Manila landing rights for a newspaper-sponsored Japanese flight to Australia. The landing-field map and its circulation from a Japanese consul through the American consular service to the U.S. Asiatic Fleet also reveal the overlap among civil aviation, military geography, diplomacy, and naval intelligence, even though the proposed flight was apparently canceled.
